source.title: Unforgettable Generalization in Language Models
source.authors: Eric Zhang; Leshem Choshen; Jacob Andreas

record.tranche_reason: Tests capability forgetting and whether task information remains recoverable, using randomized-label fine-tuning and linear probes rather than the named knowledge-unlearning methods or recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The study measures held-out task accuracy after random-label forgetting and reports linear-probe recovery. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning on a small attack set, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt variations. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study gives a new setting, skill forgetting by random-label fine-tuning on Llama2-7B. It reports held-out accuracy after forgetting (version A's near-chance part), off-target forgetting on other tasks (A's general-ability part), and linear-probe recovery after forgetting (C's blocks-access-not-deletion part). It targets capabilities, not factual knowledge or the named WMDP, WHP or RMU methods, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that dataset difficulty does not predict forgetting while hidden-state variance does. The abstract calls confidence weakly predictive; the conclusion says it is not. They conclude that random-label forgetting is shallow and that linear probes still recover correct responses.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies capability forgetting by fine-tuning on randomized task labels, not targeted factual-knowledge unlearning by gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU.
record.method_sensitivity: The degree of forgetting varies substantially by task; the authors report similar broad trends with 100 versus 1000 forgetting examples, with flipped-label fine-tuning, and across evaluated model families.

fits_no_version.finding: The degree of forgetting depends mainly on the evaluated task, not the task trained to forget. Forgetting is weakly predicted by hidden-state variance and model confidence, not task difficulty.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How well random-label forgetting generalizes is a property of the evaluated task and its representation spread, not of the forget set.

record.problems: The main experiments concern capabilities rather than factual knowledge and mostly use one model family. Probe accuracy values are presented in a figure without exact values in the text, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The probe is trained with task training data, so it is not one of the simple prompt-only recovery attacks in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: The cross-task matrices in Figures 3, 8, and 9 are not extracted cell by cell because they contain many task-pair results; the paper's explicit overall cross-task finding is recorded in cross_task_summary. The flipped-label and other-model matrix details are likewise omitted. Figure 5's learning/forgetting-order analysis is not a direct test of the listed recovery methods.

untested.parts: Targeted factual knowledge (only skills are studied). No retain-set or general-capability benchmark beyond cross-task effects. No prompt, fine-tuning or quantization recovery attacks.
No activation-direction ablation. The probe is trained on task training data, so it reads out information rather than restoring behaviour.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery.
No robust counter-method is proposed or tested.

missing.what: Pre-trained and fine-tuned accuracies and per-task forget ratios. These give the baseline for judging partial forgetting beyond the 50% chance mark.
Probe accuracy after pre-training and after fine-tuning, the comparison points for post-forgetting probe accuracy.
Single-task forget ratios for GPT-J-6B and GPT-2, and for flipped-label forgetting, which the authors say show the same trends.

record.verdict_notes: The forgetting run stops when test accuracy falls below 50% (App. A). This selects on the test set and may explain the many exact 0.50 values. Probe rows are per-task copies of one aggregate statement. The probe uses task training labels, so it shows retained information, not a behavioural recovery attack. Large and small values come from the Figure 7 table.

versions.untested_parts: It tests whether random-label fine-tuning reduces task accuracy, but not whether general ability is retained or whether simple recovery attacks fail. The experiments concern capabilities, not targeted factual knowledge.
No post-forgetting fine-tuning attack on unrelated, loosely related, or subset relearning examples.
Linear probes are trained on representations after forgetting; activation-direction ablation is not tested, and the probe result does not establish a specific blocking mechanism.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery attack.
No newer method is tested for resistance to the specified attacks.

conditions.value: cross-task evaluation across the study's tasks

rows.value: Authors report that forgetting effectiveness is largely determined by the evaluation task rather than the task used for forgetting.
rows.note: The study describes this cross-task pattern but does not provide a single aggregate numeric value.
rows.check: Random-label training on one task makes the model forget other, untargeted tasks (e.g. science-question training yields random labels on entailment). This bears on A's 'keeping general ability' part. The row should link to A, not none. Per-cell forget ratios are in Figure 3.

relation.reason: The study's own results bear on versions A and C.

tranche.reason: This is a new setting: skill forgetting by random-label fine-tuning on Llama2-7B. It gives results on held-out near-chance accuracy, off-target forgetting and probe recovery. The reader's T2 is less apt because the target is skills, not knowledge.

source_check.notes: Figure 7 values place in task order (small column, then large); all 25 row values check out. The 0.50 values at 1000 examples reflect the stop rule (test accuracy below 50%). Sets are capped at 1000 and subsampled; per-task forget-set sizes are not given. Probe results are figure-only. The abstract names physical commonsense (PIQA) and science QA (SciQ) as tasks where forgetting does not generalize.

statements.correction: arXiv:2409.02228: Llama2-7B, skill forgetting by random-label fine-tuning on binarized tasks. With a 1000-example forget set, BoolQ held-out accuracy is 0.50 against 0.50 chance. 8 of 19 tasks reach 0.50. The others stay at 0.56-0.97 (WNLI 0.97, ARC Easy 0.86, SciQ 0.76). Forgetting spreads to untargeted tasks (Fig. 3). Linear probes still recover task answers after forgetting (Fig. 6).
statements.problem: The statement gives no number or finding for this study but cites its row large_BoolQ as support for A. Its condition 'not knowledge accuracy measured against chance' does not fit: this study measures skill accuracy against 50% chance. BoolQ is also the favourable end of mixed results.

statements.correction: arXiv:2409.02228: Llama2-7B, linear probe on the fifth-last layer after random-label forgetting, 19 binary tasks. The authors say forgetting largely does not affect probe accuracy, even where outputs become random (e.g. BoolQ, CoLA, QNLI at 0.50). Per-task probe values are figure-only (Fig. 6).
statements.problem: The statement does not name or describe this study. The cited row probe_PIQA is figure-only. It also comes from a task whose outputs were not suppressed: PIQA forget accuracy is 0.69, and the abstract says forgetting on physical commonsense does not generalize.
